title: When a Prophet, a Friend, or a City Says Other Gods
summary: Moses gives three cases of people who urge Israel to worship other gods: a prophet or dreamer whose sign comes true, a close family member or friend who entices in secret, and a whole town led astray by worthless men. In each case Israel must refuse to follow and must treat the enticement as rebellion against the God who redeemed them from Egypt, punishable by death after careful investigation. Even a real miracle does not make a message true if it leads away from the LORD.
story: Chapter 12 required that Israel worship the LORD only in the place and the way he chooses. Chapter 13 deals with the next danger: voices inside Israel calling people to other gods. It follows the logic of the first commandment to its hardest conclusions. The same test for prophets returns in chapter 18, which adds that a prophet whose word fails to come true is not from God. Israel's later history is full of the very figures this chapter describes: prophets of Baal backed by a queen (1 Kings 18), kings who led whole cities into idolatry, and the constant pressure of family and neighbors to join the worship of the surrounding nations.
historical:
This chapter has one of the closest ancient parallels in Deuteronomy. The succession treaty of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon (672 BC), which bound his vassals to support his son Ashurbanipal, required them to report any word of rebellion against the crown prince, whether it came from officials, relatives, or brothers, or from prophets, ecstatics, or those who inquire of oracles. Many scholars think Deuteronomy 13 deliberately adopts the language of such Assyrian loyalty oaths and redirects it: loyalty belongs not to the king of Assyria but to the LORD. Scholars who see the book as shaped in the seventh century read this as a pointed challenge to Assyrian power during the reign of Josiah; those who date the core of Deuteronomy much earlier point to the wider tradition of treaty stipulations going back to the Hittite period. For the broader discussion of the book's date, see the note on Deuteronomy 5.

The prophets and dreamers of verse 1 were familiar figures across the ancient Near East. Letters from the city of Mari on the Euphrates, from the eighteenth century BC, report messages from prophets and dreams sent to the king. Israel was not unusual in having prophets; what this chapter adds is a test that goes beyond whether the prophecy works.
cultural:
In an ancient society, religion was bound up with family, clan, and town. Worshiping other gods was not a private preference but an act that affected the whole community's standing before the God who had made a covenant with them. That is why Deuteronomy treats enticement to idolatry the way a nation treats treason: the word used in verse 5 is sarah, revolt or rebellion. Verse 6 names the closest relationships a person had, a brother, a child, the wife of one's embrace, the friend who is as one's own soul, to show that no bond may outrank loyalty to God.

The chapter also requires due process. In the case of the town, Israel must "inquire, investigate, and interrogate thoroughly" before acting (verse 14), and later chapters require at least two or three witnesses for any capital charge (17:6; 19:15). The witness who brought the accusation had to be the first to act against the guilty (verse 9), which placed the weight of responsibility on accusers and discouraged false charges. The destroyed town was to be burned as a whole offering and never rebuilt, and no plunder could be kept, so that no one could profit from denouncing a neighbor's city.
literary: The chapter is written in the form of case law, with three cases each introduced by "if" (verses 1, 6, and 12), moving from the public figure (a prophet) to the most private relationship (a family member or friend) to the whole community (a town). Each case names the enticing words in quotation, "Let us follow other gods" or "Let us go and worship other gods," and each includes the aside that these are gods "which you have not known," contrasting them with the God who acted in Israel's history. Each case ends with a reason drawn from the exodus and the purpose of the punishment, and the refrain "you must purge the evil from among you" (verse 5) recurs through the law code.

outline.t: A prophet or dreamer who urges other gods
A family member or friend who entices in secret
A town led astray into idolatry

doctrines.note: Signs and wonders do not validate a message on their own. A prophet is tested first by whether he leads people to the God who has already revealed himself. What God has spoken governs every new claim to speak for him.
The chapter treats enticement to other gods as the most serious threat to Israel's life, graver than any outside enemy, because it breaks the covenant bond at its root.

Verse 3 says God allows false prophets to arise to test "whether you love Him with all your heart and with all your soul." Faithfulness means holding to what God has shown himself to be, even against impressive evidence and close relationships.

words.note: Navi, prophet, one who speaks on behalf of God. Deuteronomy does not dismiss prophecy; chapter 18 promises a prophet like Moses. But here it insists that prophets are accountable to the covenant. A true prophet calls people back to the God who brought them out of Egypt.

Sarah, revolt or rebellion. It describes turning aside from a rightful authority. In verse 5 the false prophet has advocated rebellion against the LORD. The word frames idolatry as political treason against the true King, not a private opinion.

Beliyya'al, worthlessness or wickedness, often in the phrase sons of beliyya'al, meaning scoundrels or worthless men (verse 13). In later Jewish writings it became a name for an evil spiritual power, and Paul uses it that way when he asks what harmony Christ has with Belial (2 Corinthians 6:15).

Ba'ar, literally to burn, and so to consume or remove completely. The refrain "purge the evil from among you" uses it to mean removing evil from the community as fire removes what it burns. Paul echoes this language when he tells the Corinthian church to remove an unrepentant man from their fellowship (1 Corinthians 5:13).

christ: Jesus warned that false messiahs and false prophets would perform great signs and wonders to mislead, if possible, even the elect (Matthew 24:24), applying the principle of this chapter: miracles do not prove a message true. Jesus also called his followers to a loyalty that outranks even family (Matthew 10:37), echoing verse 6. At the same time, some of his opponents accused Jesus himself of leading the people astray (John 7:12, 47), which shows how this chapter could be used against the one who in Christian faith is God's own Son. The New Testament applies the chapter's concern for purity through church discipline, not the death penalty. Paul borrows Deuteronomy's refrain to tell the church to put out a man living in open sin, while leaving judgment of outsiders to God (1 Corinthians 5:12-13).

hard.q: How can the Bible command the death penalty for trying to persuade someone to worship another god?
hard.a:
The chapter commands that those who entice Israel to other gods be put to death, even family members, and that an idolatrous town be destroyed. To modern readers who value freedom of religion, this is deeply troubling. Interpreters respond in several ways. Many point out that Israel was a unique covenant nation in which God was the King, so that promoting other gods was treason against the state's very foundation, comparable to how ancient and modern nations treat attempts to overthrow their government. Others stress that the laws required thorough investigation and multiple witnesses, and note that the Old Testament rarely records these laws being carried out. Others see them as belonging to a particular stage in God's dealings with his people that is not carried over into the New Testament.

Christians broadly agree that the church may not apply these penalties. The New Testament gives the church no sword; it deals with false teaching by teaching, discipline within the fellowship, and prayer, and leaves final judgment to God (1 Corinthians 5:12-13). The church's history includes periods when Christians used chapters like this to justify persecution, which most Christians today regard as a grave misreading. The chapter's lasting lesson is the seriousness of leading others away from God, not a mandate for coercion.

questions: The chapter says a prophet's sign may come true and still be false. What claims today rely on impressive results rather than faithfulness to what God has revealed?
Verse 6 names the closest human relationships as possible sources of temptation. How do you hold loyalty to God together with love for family and friends who do not share it?
The New Testament replaces the death penalty with church discipline and teaching. What does it look like for a church to take false teaching seriously without becoming harsh or coercive?
